claim: MASTL protein levels are upregulated in HEK293 cells within hours after treatment with doxorubicin (DOX).
source: As shown in Figure 1A–C, MASTL upregulation was evident in HEK293 cells treated with doxorubicin (DOX), hydroxyurea (HU), or camptothecin (CPT), generally within hours post treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating MASTL protein levels at different time points after DOX treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: MASTL protein levels are upregulated in HEK293 cells within hours after treatment with hydroxyurea (HU).
source: As shown in Figure 1A–C, MASTL upregulation was evident in HEK293 cells treated with doxorubicin (DOX), hydroxyurea (HU), or camptothecin (CPT), generally within hours post treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating MASTL protein levels at different time points after HU treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: MASTL protein levels are upregulated in HEK293 cells within hours after treatment with camptothecin (CPT).
source: As shown in Figure 1A–C, MASTL upregulation was evident in HEK293 cells treated with doxorubicin (DOX), hydroxyurea (HU), or camptothecin (CPT), generally within hours post treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating MASTL protein levels at different time points after CPT treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: MASTL accumulation after DNA damage is confirmed in SCC38 cells treated with HU.
source: MASTL accumulation was also confirmed in SCC38 cells treated with HU or ionizing radiation (IR, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B), and HeLa cells treated with DOX or HU (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A demonstrating MASTL protein levels in SCC38 cells after HU treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: MASTL accumulation after DNA damage is confirmed in SCC38 cells treated with ionizing radiation (IR).
source: MASTL accumulation was also confirmed in SCC38 cells treated with HU or ionizing radiation (IR, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B), and HeLa cells treated with DOX or HU (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B demonstrating MASTL protein levels in SCC38 cells after IR treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: MASTL accumulation after DNA damage is confirmed in HeLa cells treated with DOX.
source: MASTL accumulation was also confirmed in SCC38 cells treated with HU or ionizing radiation (IR, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B), and HeLa cells treated with DOX or HU (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C demonstrating MASTL protein levels in HeLa cells after DOX treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: MASTL accumulation after DNA damage is confirmed in HeLa cells treated with HU.
source: MASTL accumulation was also confirmed in SCC38 cells treated with HU or ionizing radiation (IR, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B), and HeLa cells treated with DOX or HU (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D demonstrating MASTL protein levels in HeLa cells after HU treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: DNA damage-induced MASTL upregulation is consistent with the activation of ATM/ATR signaling.
source: DNA damage-induced MASTL upregulation was consistent with the activation of ATM/ATR signaling (Figure 1D and E), and was not likely to be caused by the completion of DNA repair, as judged by the phosphorylation of replication protein A (RPA, Figure 1A–D), H2AX and ATM/ATR substrates (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figures 1D and 1E showing concurrent MASTL upregulation and phosphorylation of ATM/ATR substrates, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: DNA damage-induced MASTL upregulation is not likely caused by the completion of DNA repair, as judged by the phosphorylation of replication protein A (RPA).
source: DNA damage-induced MASTL upregulation was consistent with the activation of ATM/ATR signaling (Figure 1D and E), and was not likely to be caused by the completion of DNA repair, as judged by the phosphorylation of replication protein A (RPA, Figure 1A–D), H2AX and ATM/ATR substrates (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figures 1A-D showing persistent RPA phosphorylation during MASTL upregulation, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: DNA damage-induced MASTL upregulation is not likely caused by the completion of DNA repair, as judged by the phosphorylation of H2AX and ATM/ATR substrates.
source: DNA damage-induced MASTL upregulation was consistent with the activation of ATM/ATR signaling (Figure 1D and E), and was not likely to be caused by the completion of DNA repair, as judged by the phosphorylation of replication protein A (RPA, Figure 1A–D), H2AX and ATM/ATR substrates (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figures 1D and 1E showing persistent H2AX and ATM/ATR substrate phosphorylation during MASTL upregulation, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: DNA damage does not induce upregulation of CDK1/cyclin B in HeLa cells treated with DOX.
source: In contrast to MASTL, DNA damage did not induce upregulation of other cell cycle kinases that mediate mitotic progression, including CDK1/cyclin B, Aurora A, Aurora B, and PLK1, in HeLa cells treated with DOX (Figure 1F), HU (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), or SCC38 cells with HU (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1F showing no increase in CDK1/cyclin B levels after DOX treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: DNA damage does not induce upregulation of Aurora A in HeLa cells treated with DOX.
source: In contrast to MASTL, DNA damage did not induce upregulation of other cell cycle kinases that mediate mitotic progression, including CDK1/cyclin B, Aurora A, Aurora B, and PLK1, in HeLa cells treated with DOX (Figure 1F), HU (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), or SCC38 cells with HU (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1F showing no increase in Aurora A levels after DOX treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: DNA damage does not induce upregulation of Aurora B in HeLa cells treated with DOX.
source: In contrast to MASTL, DNA damage did not induce upregulation of other cell cycle kinases that mediate mitotic progression, including CDK1/cyclin B, Aurora A, Aurora B, and PLK1, in HeLa cells treated with DOX (Figure 1F), HU (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), or SCC38 cells with HU (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1F showing no increase in Aurora B levels after DOX treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: DNA damage does not induce upregulation of PLK1 in HeLa cells treated with DOX.
source: In contrast to MASTL, DNA damage did not induce upregulation of other cell cycle kinases that mediate mitotic progression, including CDK1/cyclin B, Aurora A, Aurora B, and PLK1, in HeLa cells treated with DOX (Figure 1F), HU (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), or SCC38 cells with HU (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1F showing no increase in PLK1 levels after DOX treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: HU-induced MASTL upregulation is abrogated when cells are treated with caffeine.
source: Furthermore, HU-induced MASTL upregulation was abrogated when cells were treated with caffeine (Figure 1G), indicating that DNA damage-induced ATM/ATR activation acted upstream of MASTL upregulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1G showing reduced MASTL upregulation when caffeine is added with HU, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: DNA damage-induced ATM/ATR activation acts upstream of MASTL upregulation.
source: Furthermore, HU-induced MASTL upregulation was abrogated when cells were treated with caffeine (Figure 1G), indicating that DNA damage-induced ATM/ATR activation acted upstream of MASTL upregulation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that caffeine (an ATM/ATR inhibitor) blocks MASTL upregulation, as shown in Figure 1G and stated in the text.

claim: There is no substantial increase in MASTL RNA transcripts after DNA damage.
source: We did not observe a substantial increase in MASTL RNA transcripts, suggesting MASTL regulation at the post-translational level (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data in Figure 2A showing no significant change in MASTL mRNA levels after HU treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: MASTL regulation after DNA damage occurs at the post-translational level.
source: We did not observe a substantial increase in MASTL RNA transcripts, suggesting MASTL regulation at the post-translational level (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that MASTL protein increases without corresponding mRNA increase, as shown in Figure 2A and stated in the text.

claim: Exogenous MASTL expressed from a different promoter undergoes a similar pattern of upregulation after HU.
source: Along this line, exogenous MASTL expressed from a different promoter underwent a similar pattern of upregulation after HU, as shown by immunoblotting (Figure 2B), and by direct fluorescence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2B and fluorescence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B showing upregulation of exogenous CFP-MASTL after HU treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Accumulation of exogenous MASTL occurs concurrently with activation of DNA damage signaling, measured by phosphorylation of ATM/ATR substrates.
source: Like the endogenous MASTL, accumulation of exogenous MASTL occurred concurrently with activation of DNA damage signaling, measured by phosphorylation of ATM/ATR substrates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C showing concurrent increase in CFP-MASTL and phospho-ATM/ATR substrates, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: CPT treatment in HeLa cells increases the protein stability of MASTL.
source: Indeed, CPT treatment in HeLa cells increased the protein stability of MASTL, as evaluated by the rate of protein degradation in the presence of cycloheximide (CHX), a protein synthesis inhibitor (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2C showing slower degradation of MASTL protein after CPT treatment in the presence of CHX, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: HU treatment prolongs the half-life of MASTL protein in SCC38 cells.
source: Consistently, HU treatment prolonged the half-life of MASTL protein in SCC38 and HEK293 cells (Figure 2D–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figures 2D-F showing slower degradation of MASTL protein after HU treatment in SCC38 cells, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: HU treatment prolongs the half-life of MASTL protein in HEK293 cells.
source: Consistently, HU treatment prolonged the half-life of MASTL protein in SCC38 and HEK293 cells (Figure 2D–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E showing slower degradation of MASTL protein after HU treatment in HEK293 cells, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: E6AP was revealed as a potential binding partner of MASTL in a proteomic analysis.
source: We previously performed a proteomic analysis of proteins associated with MASTL (Ren et al., 2017), and revealed E6AP as a potential binding partner of MASTL.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous proteomic study (Ren et al., 2017) and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: E6AP is encoded by gene ubiquitin-protein ligase E3A (UBE3A).
source: E6AP is encoded by gene ubiquitin-protein ligase E3A (UBE3A), and is the founding member of the HECT (homologous to E6AP C-terminus)-domain ubiquitin ligase family (Bernassola et al., 2008; Scheffner and Kumar, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Bernassola et al., 2008; Scheffner and Kumar, 2014) and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: E6AP is the founding member of the HECT-domain ubiquitin ligase family.
source: E6AP is encoded by gene ubiquitin-protein ligase E3A (UBE3A), and is the founding member of the HECT (homologous to E6AP C-terminus)-domain ubiquitin ligase family (Bernassola et al., 2008; Scheffner and Kumar, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Bernassola et al., 2008; Scheffner and Kumar, 2014) and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The association between E6AP and MASTL is confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation.
source: The association between E6AP and MASTL was confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 3A), and by pulldown of MASTL in HeLa cell lysate using recombinant E6AP (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3A showing E6AP in MASTL immunoprecipitates, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The association between E6AP and MASTL is confirmed by pulldown of MASTL in HeLa cell lysate using recombinant E6AP.
source: The association between E6AP and MASTL was confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 3A), and by pulldown of MASTL in HeLa cell lysate using recombinant E6AP (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulldown data in Figure 3B showing MASTL binding to MBP-E6AP, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: A direct interaction between purified E6AP and MASTL proteins is evident.
source: A direct interaction between purified E6AP and MASTL proteins was also evident (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro pulldown data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A showing binding between purified MBP-E6AP and GST-MASTL, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The N-terminal region of MASTL mediates E6AP interaction in HeLa cells.
source: Further analyses using various segments of MASTL showed that the N-terminal region of MASTL mediated E6AP interaction in HeLa cells and Xenopus egg extracts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and pulldown data in Figure 3C showing E6AP binding to the N-terminal segment of MASTL, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The N-terminal region of MASTL mediates E6AP interaction in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: Further analyses using various segments of MASTL showed that the N-terminal region of MASTL mediated E6AP interaction in HeLa cells and Xenopus egg extracts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulldown data in Figure 3C showing E6AP binding to the N-terminal segment of MASTL in Xenopus egg extracts, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The N-terminus of E6AP co-immunoprecipitates MASTL.
source: On the other hand, the N-terminus of E6AP co-immunoprecipitated MASTL (Figure 3D); the MASTL-binding region was further mapped to aa 208–280 within the N-terminus of E6AP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3D showing MASTL binding to the N-terminal segment of E6AP, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The MASTL-binding region of E6AP is mapped to aa 208–280 within the N-terminus of E6AP.
source: On the other hand, the N-terminus of E6AP co-immunoprecipitated MASTL (Figure 3D); the MASTL-binding region was further mapped to aa 208–280 within the N-terminus of E6AP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C showing MASTL binding to the N3 segment (aa 108-280) of E6AP, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: E6AP depletion leads to an increased level of MASTL protein.
source: As shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, E6AP depletion led to an increased level of MASTL protein, without significant change in the MASTL mRNA level.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 4A showing increased MASTL protein after E6AP siRNA treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: E6AP depletion does not cause significant change in the MASTL mRNA level.
source: As shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, E6AP depletion led to an increased level of MASTL protein, without significant change in the MASTL mRNA level.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A showing no significant change in MASTL mRNA after E6AP siRNA treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Ectopic expression of E6AP reduces MASTL expression.
source: Ectopic expression of E6AP reduced MASTL expression, as shown by immunoblotting (Figure 4B) and immunofluorescence (IF) (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 4B and immunofluorescence data in Figure 4C showing decreased MASTL levels when HA-E6AP is overexpressed, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene deletion of E6AP augments MASTL level.
source: Consistently, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene deletion of E6AP also augmented MASTL level, in a manner that was reversed by re-expression of exogenous E6AP (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 4D showing increased MASTL levels in E6AP KO cells, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Re-expression of exogenous E6AP reverses the augmentation of MASTL level caused by E6AP gene deletion.
source: Consistently, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene deletion of E6AP also augmented MASTL level, in a manner that was reversed by re-expression of exogenous E6AP (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 4D showing decreased MASTL levels when HA-E6AP is re-expressed in E6AP KO cells, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: E6AP depletion increases the protein stability of MASTL.
source: E6AP depletion increased, and overexpression reduced, the protein stability of MASTL (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase data in Figures 4E and F showing slower degradation of MASTL protein after E6AP siRNA treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: E6AP overexpression reduces the protein stability of MASTL.
source: E6AP depletion increased, and overexpression reduced, the protein stability of MASTL (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase data in Figures 4E and F showing faster degradation of MASTL protein after E6AP overexpression, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: E6AP depletion disrupts MASTL ubiquitination in HeLa cells.
source: Furthermore, E6AP depletion disrupted MASTL ubiquitination in HeLa cells (Figure 4G), indicating that E6AP mediated the ubiquitination of MASTL.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4G showing reduced ubiquitinated MASTL in E6AP KO cells, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: E6AP mediates the ubiquitination of MASTL.
source: Furthermore, E6AP depletion disrupted MASTL ubiquitination in HeLa cells (Figure 4G), indicating that E6AP mediated the ubiquitination of MASTL.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that E6AP depletion reduces MASTL ubiquitination, as shown in Figure 4G and stated in the text.

claim: E6AP depletion does not further increase MASTL level in cells treated with MG132.
source: Consistently, E6AP depletion did not further increase MASTL level in cells treated with MG132 to suppress proteasome-mediated protein degradation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B showing similar MASTL levels in control and E6AP KO cells when treated with MG132, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: An in vitro ubiquitination assay confirms MASTL as an effective substrate of E6AP.
source: An in vitro ubiquitination assay also confirmed MASTL as an effective substrate of E6AP (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro ubiquitination data in Figure 4H showing ubiquitination of MASTL by E6AP, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: MASTL ubiquitination is specifically mediated by E6AP in the in vitro ubiquitination assay.
source: MASTL ubiquitination was specifically mediated by E6AP in the assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C); the MASTL mutant deleted of the E6AP-binding motif was not ubiquitinated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro ubiquitination data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C showing MASTL ubiquitination only when E6AP is present, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The MASTL mutant deleted of the E6AP-binding motif is not ubiquitinated.
source: MASTL ubiquitination was specifically mediated by E6AP in the assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C); the MASTL mutant deleted of the E6AP-binding motif was not ubiquitinated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro ubiquitination data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D showing no ubiquitination of ΔN MASTL (lacking E6AP-binding domain), and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: MASTL depletion substantially hinders DNA damage recovery.
source: MASTL depletion substantially hindered DNA damage recovery, whereas E6AP knockout (KO) accelerated mitotic entry after DNA damage (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by mitotic index data in Figure 5A showing reduced mitotic entry in MASTL knockdown cells after etoposide release, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: E6AP knockout accelerates mitotic entry after DNA damage.
source: MASTL depletion substantially hindered DNA damage recovery, whereas E6AP knockout (KO) accelerated mitotic entry after DNA damage (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by mitotic index data in Figure 5A showing increased mitotic entry in E6AP KO cells after etoposide release, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The recovery of mitotic entry in E6AP KO cells is disrupted by MASTL downregulation.
source: The recovery of mitotic entry in E6AP KO cells was disrupted by MASTL downregulation, indicating its dependence on MASTL (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by mitotic index data in Figure 5A showing reduced mitotic entry in E6AP KO cells when MASTL is knocked down, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: MASTL depletion causes prolonged cell cycle arrest after HU treatment.
source: MASTL depletion caused prolonged cell cycle arrest; loss of E6AP promoted cell cycle recovery; and suppression of MASTL in E6AP-deleted cells abrogated cell cycle progression (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data in Figure 5B showing prolonged G2/M arrest in MASTL knockdown cells after HU release, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Loss of E6AP promotes cell cycle recovery after HU treatment.
source: MASTL depletion caused prolonged cell cycle arrest; loss of E6AP promoted cell cycle recovery; and suppression of MASTL in E6AP-deleted cells abrogated cell cycle progression (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data in Figure 5B showing faster cell cycle progression in E6AP KO cells after HU release, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Suppression of MASTL in E6AP-deleted cells abrogates cell cycle progression after HU treatment.
source: MASTL depletion caused prolonged cell cycle arrest; loss of E6AP promoted cell cycle recovery; and suppression of MASTL in E6AP-deleted cells abrogated cell cycle progression (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data in Figure 5B showing impaired cell cycle progression in E6AP KO cells when MASTL is knocked down after HU release, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: MASTL knockdown does not significantly disrupt cell proliferation under the unperturbed condition.
source: By comparison, MASTL knockdown did not significantly disrupt cell proliferation under the unperturbed condition (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell proliferation data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A showing similar cell numbers in control and MASTL knockdown cells without DNA damage, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: E6AP knockout in HEK293 cells reduces DNA damage checkpoint signaling after DOX treatment.
source: Interestingly, KO of E6AP in HEK293 cells reduced DNA damage checkpoint signaling, measured by phosphorylation of SMC1, CHK1, CHK2, H2AX, and pan-ATM/ATR substrates after DOX treatment (Figure 5C), and by phosphorylation of pan-ATM/ATR substrates after ETO (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 5C showing reduced phosphorylation of checkpoint proteins in E6AP KO cells after DOX treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: E6AP knockout in HEK293 cells reduces DNA damage checkpoint signaling after ETO treatment.
source: Interestingly, KO of E6AP in HEK293 cells reduced DNA damage checkpoint signaling, measured by phosphorylation of SMC1, CHK1, CHK2, H2AX, and pan-ATM/ATR substrates after DOX treatment (Figure 5C), and by phosphorylation of pan-ATM/ATR substrates after ETO (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B showing reduced phosphorylation of ATM/ATR substrates in E6AP KO cells after ETO treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: A similar deficiency of ATM/ATR-mediated phosphorylation is observed in HeLa cells with E6AP gene deletion.
source: A similar deficiency of ATM/ATR-mediated phosphorylation was observed in HeLa cells with E6AP gene deletion, which was rescued by E6AP re-expression (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 5D showing reduced phosphorylation of ATM/ATR substrates in E6AP KO HeLa cells after ETO treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The deficiency of ATM/ATR-mediated phosphorylation in E6AP KO HeLa cells is rescued by E6AP re-expression.
source: A similar deficiency of ATM/ATR-mediated phosphorylation was observed in HeLa cells with E6AP gene deletion, which was rescued by E6AP re-expression (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 5D showing restored phosphorylation of ATM/ATR substrates when HA-E6AP is re-expressed in E6AP KO cells, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: ATM/ATR-mediated substrate phosphorylation in E6AP KO cells is restored by MASTL depletion.
source: Interestingly, ATM/ATR-mediated substrate phosphorylation in E6AP KO cells was also restored by MASTL depletion, indicating that E6AP promoted DNA damage checkpoint signaling by counteracting MASTL (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 5E showing restored phosphorylation of ATM/ATR substrates in E6AP KO cells when MASTL is knocked down, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: E6AP promotes DNA damage checkpoint signaling by counteracting MASTL.
source: Interestingly, ATM/ATR-mediated substrate phosphorylation in E6AP KO cells was also restored by MASTL depletion, indicating that E6AP promoted DNA damage checkpoint signaling by counteracting MASTL (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that MASTL depletion rescues checkpoint signaling defects in E6AP KO cells, as shown in Figure 5E and stated in the text.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation of E6AP with CFP-MASTL is profoundly disrupted by HU treatment.
source: Interestingly, co-immunoprecipitation of E6AP with CPF-MASTL was profoundly disrupted by HU treatment (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6A showing reduced E6AP binding to CFP-MASTL after HU treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The loss of E6AP and MASTL association after DNA damage is a result of active DNA damage signaling.
source: This loss of E6AP and MASTL association was a result of active DNA damage signaling, as inhibition of ATM/ATR by caffeine preserved this protein association in the presence of HU (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6B showing preserved E6AP-MASTL binding when caffeine is added with HU, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Inhibition of ATM/ATR by caffeine preserves E6AP and MASTL association in the presence of HU.
source: This loss of E6AP and MASTL association was a result of active DNA damage signaling, as inhibition of ATM/ATR by caffeine preserved this protein association in the presence of HU (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6B showing preserved E6AP-MASTL binding when caffeine is added with HU, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: E6AP possesses a single evolutionally conserved serine, Ser-218 in humans, as a potential consensus site of ATM/ATR-mediated phosphorylation.
source: E6AP possesses a single evolutionally conserved serine, Ser-218 in humans, as a potential consensus site of ATM/ATR-mediated phosphorylation (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data in Figure 7A showing conserved SQ motif at position 218 in human E6AP, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation is documented in multiple proteomic databases.
source: E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation was also documented in multiple proteomic databases (Beli et al., 2012; Franz-Wachtel et al., 2012; Kettenbach et al., 2011; Klammer et al., 2012; Matsuoka et al., 2007; Olsen et al., 2010; Schweppe et al., 2013; Weber et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple proteomic studies and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation is induced after HU treatment.
source: We generated a phospho-specific antibody for this residue, and observed the induction of Ser-218 phosphorylation after HU (Figure 7B), or DOX treatment (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 7B showing increased phospho-E6AP Ser-218 signal after HU treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation is induced after DOX treatment.
source: We generated a phospho-specific antibody for this residue, and observed the induction of Ser-218 phosphorylation after HU (Figure 7B), or DOX treatment (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 7C showing increased phospho-E6AP Ser-218 signal after DOX treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The phospho-E6AP Ser-218 signal is absent in E6AP KO cells.
source: This phospho-signal was absent in E6AP KO cells (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), and was diminished with S218A mutation (Figure 7E), confirming its specificity.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A showing no phospho-E6AP Ser-218 signal in E6AP KO cells, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The phospho-E6AP Ser-218 signal is diminished with S218A mutation.
source: This phospho-signal was absent in E6AP KO cells (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), and was diminished with S218A mutation (Figure 7E), confirming its specificity.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 7E showing no phospho-E6AP Ser-218 signal in S218A mutant, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Inhibition of ATM using a selective kinase inhibitor reduces E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation after DOX treatment in HeLa cells.
source: Inhibition of ATM using a selective kinase inhibitor reduced E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation after DOX treatment in both HeLa and HEK293 cells (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 7C showing reduced phospho-E6AP Ser-218 signal when ATM inhibitor is added with DOX in HeLa cells, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Inhibition of ATM using a selective kinase inhibitor reduces E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation after DOX treatment in HEK293 cells.
source: Inhibition of ATM using a selective kinase inhibitor reduced E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation after DOX treatment in both HeLa and HEK293 cells (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B showing reduced phospho-E6AP Ser-218 signal when ATM inhibitor is added with DOX in HEK293 cells, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: ATM is the primary kinase to mediate E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation in response to HU.
source: ATM was also the primary kinase to mediate E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation in response to HU (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C showing reduced phospho-E6AP Ser-218 signal when ATM inhibitor is added with HU, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The phospho-mimetic mutant form of E6AP, E6AP S218D, exhibits significantly reduced association with MASTL compared to WT E6AP.
source: Indeed, the phospho-mimetic mutant form of E6AP, E6AP S218D, exhibited significantly reduced association with MASTL, compared to WT or phospho-deficient S218A E6AP (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7D showing reduced MASTL binding to S218D E6AP compared to WT, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The phospho-mimetic mutant form of E6AP, E6AP S218D, exhibits significantly reduced association with MASTL compared to S218A E6AP.
source: Indeed, the phospho-mimetic mutant form of E6AP, E6AP S218D, exhibited significantly reduced association with MASTL, compared to WT or phospho-deficient S218A E6AP (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7D showing reduced MASTL binding to S218D E6AP compared to S218A, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: DNA damage disrupts MASTL association with WT E6AP.
source: Furthermore, DNA damage disrupted MASTL association with WT E6AP, but not E6AP S218A (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7E showing reduced MASTL binding to WT E6AP after DOX treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: DNA damage does not disrupt MASTL association with E6AP S218A.
source: Furthermore, DNA damage disrupted MASTL association with WT E6AP, but not E6AP S218A (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7E showing preserved MASTL binding to S218A E6AP after DOX treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: S218A mutation prevents MASTL protein accumulation after DNA damage.
source: Consistent with the persistent MASTL association, S218A mutation also prevented MASTL protein accumulation after DNA damage (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 7F showing no increase in MASTL levels in cells expressing S218A E6AP after DOX treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Cells expressing S218A E6AP exhibit defective DNA damage checkpoint recovery compared to cells expressing WT E6AP, as measured by mitotic index after ETO release.
source: Interestingly, using both mitotic index measurement after ETO release, or cell cycle profiling after HU, we noted defective DNA damage checkpoint recovery in cells harboring E6AP S218A mutation (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mitotic index data in Figure 8A showing reduced mitotic entry in cells expressing S218A E6AP after ETO release, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Cells expressing S218A E6AP exhibit defective DNA damage checkpoint recovery compared to cells expressing WT E6AP, as measured by cell cycle profiling after HU.
source: Interestingly, using both mitotic index measurement after ETO release, or cell cycle profiling after HU, we noted defective DNA damage checkpoint recovery in cells harboring E6AP S218A mutation (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data in Figure 8B showing delayed cell cycle progression in cells expressing S218A E6AP after HU release, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Cells expressing S218A E6AP exhibit defective resumption of cell cycle progression post DNA damage, as assessed by phosphorylation of CDK substrates.
source: The resumption of cell cycle progression post DNA damage was also assessed biochemically, by phosphorylation of CDK substrates, and a similar pattern of deficiency was seen with S218A mutation (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 8C showing reduced phospho-CDK substrate levels in cells expressing S218A E6AP after ETO release, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Cells expressing S218A E6AP exhibit elevated levels of DNA damage signaling compared to cells expressing WT E6AP.
source: Furthermore, cells expressing S218A E6AP, compared to those expressing WT E6AP, exhibited elevated levels of DNA damage signaling (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 8D showing increased phosphorylation of ATM/ATR substrates and SMC1 in cells expressing S218A E6AP after CPT treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: DNA damage-induced MASTL upregulation is unique among mitotic kinases.
source: DNA damage-induced MASTL upregulation was caused by decreased protein degradation, and was unique among mitotic kinases.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by data showing other mitotic kinases (CDK1/cyclin B, Aurora A/B, PLK1) do not exhibit similar upregulation.

claim: DNA damage-induced MASTL upregulation is caused by decreased protein degradation.
source: DNA damage-induced MASTL upregulation was caused by decreased protein degradation, and was unique among mitotic kinases.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by cycloheximide chase experiments showing increased MASTL protein stability after DNA damage.

claim: E6AP is the E3 ubiquitin ligase that mediates MASTL degradation.
source: We identified E6AP as the E3 ubiquitin ligase that mediated MASTL degradation.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experiments showing E6AP-mediated MASTL ubiquitination and degradation.

claim: MASTL degradation is inhibited upon DNA damage as a result of the dissociation of E6AP from MASTL.
source: MASTL degradation was inhibited upon DNA damage as a result of the dissociation of E6AP from MASTL.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing reduced E6AP-MASTL binding after DNA damage.

claim: E6AP depletion reduces DNA damage signaling.
source: E6AP depletion reduced DNA damage signaling, and promoted cell cycle recovery from the DNA damage checkpoint, in a MASTL-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by immunoblotting data showing reduced phosphorylation of checkpoint proteins in E6AP KO cells.

claim: E6AP depletion promotes cell cycle recovery from the DNA damage checkpoint in a MASTL-dependent manner.
source: E6AP depletion reduced DNA damage signaling, and promoted cell cycle recovery from the DNA damage checkpoint, in a MASTL-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by cell cycle profiling data showing faster recovery in E6AP KO cells that is reversed by MASTL knockdown.

claim: E6AP is phosphorylated at Ser-218 by ATM after DNA damage.
source: Furthermore, we found that E6AP was phosphorylated at Ser-218 by ATM after DNA damage and that this phosphorylation was required for its dissociation from MASTL, the stabilization of MASTL, and the timely recovery of cell cycle progression.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by immunoblotting data showing E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation after DNA damage that is reduced by ATM inhibition.

claim: E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation is required for its dissociation from MASTL.
source: Furthermore, we found that E6AP was phosphorylated at Ser-218 by ATM after DNA damage and that this phosphorylation was required for its dissociation from MASTL, the stabilization of MASTL, and the timely recovery of cell cycle progression.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by immunoprecipitation data showing that S218A mutation prevents DNA damage-induced dissociation of E6AP from MASTL.

claim: E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation is required for the stabilization of MASTL.
source: Furthermore, we found that E6AP was phosphorylated at Ser-218 by ATM after DNA damage and that this phosphorylation was required for its dissociation from MASTL, the stabilization of MASTL, and the timely recovery of cell cycle progression.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by immunoblotting data showing that S218A mutation prevents MASTL accumulation after DNA damage.

claim: E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation is required for the timely recovery of cell cycle progression.
source: Furthermore, we found that E6AP was phosphorylated at Ser-218 by ATM after DNA damage and that this phosphorylation was required for its dissociation from MASTL, the stabilization of MASTL, and the timely recovery of cell cycle progression.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by cell cycle profiling data showing delayed recovery in cells expressing S218A E6AP.

claim: ATM/ATR-dependent signaling, while activating the DNA damage checkpoint, also initiates cell cycle recovery from the arrest.
source: Together, our data revealed that ATM/ATR-dependent signaling, while activating the DNA damage checkpoint, also initiates cell cycle recovery from the arrest.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the abstract and is inferred from the finding that ATM phosphorylates E6AP to promote MASTL stabilization and checkpoint recovery.

claim: The ATM-E6AP-MASTL axis results in a timer-like mechanism that ensures the transient nature of the DNA damage checkpoint.
source: Consequently, this results in a timer-like mechanism that ensures the transient nature of the DNA damage checkpoint.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the abstract and is inferred from the observation that ATM activation simultaneously activates checkpoint and initiates recovery mechanisms.

claim: DNA damage activates ATM and ATR kinases.
source: Upon DNA damage, ATM and ATR phosphorylate and activate checkpoint kinases CHK1 and CHK2, which, in turn, inhibit CDC25 to prevent activation of cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) (Shiloh, 2003; Zhou and Elledge, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Shiloh, 2003; Zhou and Elledge, 2000) and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: ATM and ATR phosphorylate and activate checkpoint kinases CHK1 and CHK2.
source: Upon DNA damage, ATM and ATR phosphorylate and activate checkpoint kinases CHK1 and CHK2, which, in turn, inhibit CDC25 to prevent activation of cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) (Shiloh, 2003; Zhou and Elledge, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Shiloh, 2003; Zhou and Elledge, 2000) and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: CHK1 and CHK2 inhibit CDC25 to prevent activation of cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs).
source: Upon DNA damage, ATM and ATR phosphorylate and activate checkpoint kinases CHK1 and CHK2, which, in turn, inhibit CDC25 to prevent activation of cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) (Shiloh, 2003; Zhou and Elledge, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Shiloh, 2003; Zhou and Elledge, 2000) and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: MASTL has been characterized as an important regulator of mitosis.
source: Microtubule-associated serine/threonine kinase-like (MASTL, also known as Greatwall) has been characterized as an important regulator of mitosis.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and represents established scientific knowledge about MASTL function.

claim: MASTL is activated during mitotic entry.
source: Like CDK1 and other mitotic kinases, MASTL is activated during mitotic entry, and the kinase activity of MASTL promotes mitosis, although mitotic entry is still permitted in mammalian cells depleted of MASTL (Archambault et al., 2007; Blake-Hodek et al., 2012; Castilho et al., 2009; Peng and Maller, 2010; Vigneron et al., 2011; Voets and Wolthuis, 2010; Wang et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2004; Yu et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations and represents established scientific knowledge about MASTL function.

claim: The kinase activity of MASTL promotes mitosis.
source: Like CDK1 and other mitotic kinases, MASTL is activated during mitotic entry, and the kinase activity of MASTL promotes mitosis, although mitotic entry is still permitted in mammalian cells depleted of MASTL (Archambault et al., 2007; Blake-Hodek et al., 2012; Castilho et al., 2009; Peng and Maller, 2010; Vigneron et al., 2011; Voets and Wolthuis, 2010; Wang et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2004; Yu et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations and represents established scientific knowledge about MASTL function.

claim: Mitotic entry is still permitted in mammalian cells depleted of MASTL.
source: Like CDK1 and other mitotic kinases, MASTL is activated during mitotic entry, and the kinase activity of MASTL promotes mitosis, although mitotic entry is still permitted in mammalian cells depleted of MASTL (Archambault et al., 2007; Blake-Hodek et al., 2012; Castilho et al., 2009; Peng and Maller, 2010; Vigneron et al., 2011; Voets and Wolthuis, 2010; Wang et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2004; Yu et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations and represents established scientific knowledge about MASTL function.

claim: MASTL phosphorylates α-endosulfine (ENSA) and cyclic AMP-regulated 19 kDa phosphoprotein (ARPP19).
source: Upon activation, MASTL phosphorylates α-endosulfine (ENSA) and cyclic AMP-regulated 19 kDa phosphoprotein (ARPP19) which then inhibit PP2A/B55 (protein phosphatase 2A/B55 targeting subunit).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and represents established scientific knowledge about MASTL substrates.

claim: Phosphorylated ENSA and ARPP19 inhibit PP2A/B55.
source: Upon activation, MASTL phosphorylates α-endosulfine (ENSA) and cyclic AMP-regulated 19 kDa phosphoprotein (ARPP19) which then inhibit PP2A/B55 (protein phosphatase 2A/B55 targeting subunit).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and represents established scientific knowledge about ENSA/ARPP19 function.

claim: PP2A/B55 functions as the principal phosphatase catalyzing the dephosphorylation of CDK substrates.
source: Because PP2A/B55 functions as the principal phosphatase catalyzing the dephosphorylation of CDK substrates, the coordination between the kinase activity of MASTL with that of CDK1 enables substrate phosphorylation and mitotic progression (Castilho et al., 2009; Gharbi-Ayachi et al., 2010; Mochida et al., 2009; Mochida et al., 2010; Vigneron et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations and represents established scientific knowledge about PP2A/B55 function.

claim: MASTL is required for cell cycle recovery from the DNA damage checkpoint in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: Interestingly, in addition to its mitotic function, MASTL is also required for cell cycle recovery from the DNA damage checkpoint in Xenopus egg extracts (Medema, 2010; Peng et al., 2011; Peng et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Medema, 2010; Peng et al., 2011; Peng et al., 2010) and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Addition of MASTL in Xenopus egg extracts facilitates DNA damage checkpoint recovery.
source: Addition of MASTL in extracts facilitated, and depletion of MASTL hindered, DNA damage checkpoint recovery, as evidenced by both mitotic phosphorylation of CDK substrates and de-activation of checkpoint signaling (Peng et al., 2011; Peng et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Peng et al., 2011; Peng et al., 2010) and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Depletion of MASTL in Xenopus egg extracts hinders DNA damage checkpoint recovery.
source: Addition of MASTL in extracts facilitated, and depletion of MASTL hindered, DNA damage checkpoint recovery, as evidenced by both mitotic phosphorylation of CDK substrates and de-activation of checkpoint signaling (Peng et al., 2011; Peng et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Peng et al., 2011; Peng et al., 2010) and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Ectopic expression of MASTL in human cells promotes cell proliferation under DNA damage.
source: Consistently, ectopic expression of MASTL in human cells promoted cell proliferation under DNA damage (Wang et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Wang et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2016) and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Mutations of E6AP cause Angelman syndrome in humans.
source: Mutations of E6AP cause Angelman syndrome, a debilitating neurological disorder in humans (Bernassola et al., 2008; Buiting et al., 2016; Levav-Cohen et al., 2012; Sell and Margolis, 2015; Wolyniec et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations and represents established scientific knowledge about E6AP and Angelman syndrome.

claim: Mouse embryo fibroblasts lacking E6AP escape replicative senescence.
source: Interestingly, mouse embryo fibroblasts lacking E6AP escaped replicative senescence, proliferated under stress conditions, supported anchorage-independent growth, and enhanced tumor growth in vivo (Levav-Cohen et al., 2012; Wolyniec et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Levav-Cohen et al., 2012; Wolyniec et al., 2013) and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Mouse embryo fibroblasts lacking E6AP proliferate under stress conditions.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Levav-Cohen et al., 2012; Wolyniec et al., 2013) and is explicitly stated in the text.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Levav-Cohen et al., 2012; Wolyniec et al., 2013) and is explicitly stated in the text.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Levav-Cohen et al., 2012; Wolyniec et al., 2013) and is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The phenotypes of E6AP-deficient mouse embryo fibroblasts can be potentially attributed to MASTL upregulation.
source: These phenotypes are not well explained in the context of known substrates of E6AP (Sell and Margolis, 2015), but can be potentially attributed to MASTL upregulation, as characterized in our current study.
evidence: The claim is speculative and inferred from the findings of the current study showing E6AP regulates MASTL stability.

claim: ATM-mediated MASTL upregulation may provide an initial signal to trigger positive feedback reactions that shift the balance from cell cycle arrest to recovery.
source: We speculate that, in the case of DNA damage recovery, ATM-mediated MASTL upregulation may provide an initial signal to trigger these positive feedback reactions, ultimately shifting the balance from cell cycle arrest to recovery.
evidence: The claim is speculative and represents a proposed model based on the findings of the study.

claim: The timer-like mechanism can contribute to the transient nature of the DNA damage checkpoint.
source: Of note, this timer-like mechanism can contribute to the transient nature of the DNA damage checkpoint, as observed in yeast, frog, and mammalian cells (Bartek and Lukas, 2007; Clémenson and Marsolier-Kergoat, 2009; Syljuåsen, 2007; van Vugt et al., 2004a; Yoo et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the findings and supported by citations to previous observations of transient checkpoint arrest.

claim: The impact of MASTL upregulation on promoting checkpoint recovery and cell cycle progression can be attributed to inhibition of PP2A/B55.
source: The subsequent impact of MASTL upregulation on promoting checkpoint recovery and cell cycle progression can be attributed to inhibition of PP2A/B55, although the potential involvement of additional mechanisms is not excluded.
evidence: The claim is inferred from established knowledge about MASTL function and the findings of the study, with acknowledgment of potential additional mechanisms.

claim: MASTL kinase has emerged as an important factor of tumorigenesis and treatment resistance in multiple types of cancer.
source: MASTL kinase has emerged as an important factor of tumorigenesis and treatment resistance in multiple types of cancer (Fatima et al., 2020; Marzec and Burgess, 2018; Wang et al., 2014).
